analysis.one_liner: Exempts repackaged versions of old drugs from Medicaid and Medicare rebates.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 1, 2025 with one cosponsor and referred to two House committees; no hearing, markup, or vote has followed.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug companies owe rebates to Medicaid and Medicare when they sell a new version of an old drug, such as a new extended-release pill. This bill lets a manufacturer ask the government to label such a version a "priority research drug" instead, as long as the original drug is at least 10 years old, the company is studying it for a new use, and that new use would mostly be billed to federal health programs. Labeled that way, the drug no longer counts as a line extension, so the manufacturer pays the specialized rebates and the federal government cannot treat its older price as the floor for calculating rebates.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of long-approved drugs that are developing a new formulation or new use. They keep selling the product to Medicaid and Medicare while paying less in rebates, and the company's older, lower price no longer drags down the rebate calculations for the new version.

how_it_helps.text: A manufacturer can request that a drug otherwise treated as a line extension be designated a priority research drug, removing it from the specialized line-extension rebates under the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program and the Medicare inflation rebate program [S2].

To qualify, the drug must have been approved at least 10 years earlier, the manufacturer must be investigating a new use for which no alternative drug is approved, and the new use must target a condition where at least a third of patient claims were paid by Medicaid, CHIP, subsidized Medicare drug coverage, the 340B discount program, or the VA [S2] [S3].
The bill also excludes priority research drugs from the Medicaid "best price" special rule for selected drugs and from the Medicare definition of a line extension [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicaid (state and federal budgets) and Medicare, through rebates the manufacturers no longer owe — a cost borne by taxpayers and, on the Medicaid side, state budgets. Patients pay through the public dollars that fund these programs.

drawbacks.text: The bill reduces rebates paid to Medicaid and Medicare for certain drugs, which increases the cost those public programs bear [S2].

Qualification requires only that the manufacturer be investigating a new use, not that any new use ever be approved, so a company could win the rebate exemption for a reformulated old drug without ever delivering the promised new cure [S2] [S3].

The bill's supporters would argue that forgone rebates are justified if they unlock treatments for conditions with no approved drug today, but the bill does not condition the exemption on the new use actually reaching patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is indirect and speculative: a company might keep investing in an old drug's new use because it keeps more revenue. The cost is direct and certain: smaller rebates for Medicaid and Medicare on drugs these programs already buy. Because the exemption is not tied to the new use being approved or reaching patients, the design lets manufacturers capture the financial benefit without a guarantee of the promised medical benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and neither has taken it up since [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Davis (D-NC) introduced the bill on April 1, 2025, joined by Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX), for a total of one cosponsor [S3] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction [S1] [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has happened, so no one has gained or lost anything yet; the bill's manufacturer-facing terms exist only on paper.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill is dormant

for.name: August Pfluger
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, its only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan at one member per party — a Democrat sponsored it and a single Republican cosponsored it — and no one has voted on it, so no partisan split is on record.

industries.note: The bill lets manufacturers of long-approved drugs escape the extra rebates owed when they sell a new formulation of an old drug, while Medicaid and Medicare keep buying it. The savings come out of public programs' budgets, so the industry's gain is the public's cost.

industries.industry: State Medicaid programs and federal taxpayers
industries.note: Forgone line-extension and inflation rebates would raise the cost of the same drugs to Medicaid and Medicare, meaning more public spending for the same medicines. States share the Medicaid cost directly.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no committee action in months, and jurisdiction split between two committees, the bill's realistic path is to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless the sponsor builds cosponsor support or a committee takes an interest.
